title: not certainty
hookLine: not certainty; a mustard seed, and a father who believed and doubted at once

cards: You pray, and feel nothing. You sit in a service where everyone around you seems moved, and wonder what you're missing.
Next to people whose faith looks like a wall, solid and never shaken, it's easy to decide faith belongs to other people. Here's a scene from Mark's Gospel.

A father brings his son, who has suffered since childhood, and the disciples couldn't help. The father says: if you can do anything, help us. Jesus tells him all things are possible to the one who believes.
And the father cries out, in tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once.

teach.b: Faith. The Greek word is pistis, and it's less about certainty than about trust. It's the word for trusting a friend, or being faithful to one.

You have faith in someone the way you have faith in a bridge: not because you've proved it, but because you're willing to put your weight on it. Amen, on day eight, came from a root meaning firm, solid. Same idea.
Now, how much of it do you need? Another Gospel tells the same story, and afterward the disciples ask why they couldn't help the boy.
Jesus answers: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." He doesn't say: if you had enormous faith.
He says: if you had even this much. The mountain is big. The seed is tiny.
A letter in the Bible puts it another way: "faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." Not seen. And not always felt.
Mother Teresa's private letters, published after her death, describe years of feeling God's absence when she prayed. She kept praying.
And doubt sat in the very first congregation: after Easter, one Gospel says the disciples saw Jesus on a mountain, and "they worshipped him: but some doubted."
So some Christian writers have said that doubt, and even dryness, isn't simply faith's opposite.
The father in Mark didn't bring a perfect faith. He brought a half-sure, crying, both-at-once faith, and the story doesn't send him away. Jesus heals the boy.

how: Christians describe faith as trust in God, and in times of doubt or dryness some pray the father's line from Mark: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief

s: in the Bible, faith means being certain
the Greek pistis is trust and faithfulness: putting your weight on something you can't prove.
Jesus said you'd need great faith to move a mountain
he said faith as small as a grain of mustard seed.
Mother Teresa wrote of years of feeling God's absence in prayer
her private letters, published after her death, say so. she kept praying.

games.q: your son has suffered since he was a child. Jesus says all things are possible to the one who believes. you're not sure you do. what do you say?
o: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
games.why: the father says both at once, belief and unbelief, and the story doesn't turn him away: Jesus heals the boy.

practice: Here's the practice. If there's something tiny nearby, a grain of rice, a seed, a crumb, put it in your palm. If not, just open your hand.
Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're unsure about. Don't solve it.
Just admit it. Now think of one small thing you do trust: the floor holding you up, the next breath coming, one person. Let that small thing be enough, for now.
If you pray, the father's words are there for you: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.

wordCard.voice: Faith. Pistis. Not certainty: trust, even the size of a seed. Sixteenth word.

orig.note: Greek. faith, trust, faithfulness. the same word covers trusting someone and being loyal to them.

carryVoice: Your line: small is enough. On a day you feel nothing, a seed's worth still counts. Day sixteen.
